analysis.one_liner: Requires large companies to audit supply chains annually for child and forced labor and post results online.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote and died without a single cosponsor after being referred to a House subcommittee.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies with over $1 billion in annual revenue would have to hire an independent auditor every year to check whether their supply chains use child labor or forced labor. They would report the finding to the Labor Department and the SEC, and post a notice on their website homepage either that their products are "free of child labor and forced labor" or that their products "may have been produced using child labor or forced labor." The bill covers manufactured goods, farm commodities, and oil, gas, and minerals, and applies all the way down the chain to suppliers the company has no direct relationship with. It creates no penalties, only a disclosure requirement.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who want to avoid buying goods made with child or forced labor, and workers who toil under those conditions, would gain a new, public source of information. Reputational exposure would give large companies a reason to clean up their supply chains.

how_it_helps.text: Companies with over $1 billion in gross annual revenues would have to submit to an annual independent audit of their supply chains for child labor and forced labor, conducted in the first quarter of each fiscal year.

Each company would have to report the auditor's determination to the Department of Labor and the Securities and Exchange Commission within 60 days, and post a clear notice on its website homepage stating either "Products are free of child labor and forced labor" or "Products may have been produced using child labor or forced labor."
The audit covers the entire supply chain, including labor recruiters, suppliers of components and raw materials, and suppliers the company has no direct relationship with.
The bill defines child labor and forced labor by reference to international labor standards, including International Labor Organization Conventions 182 and 29.

analysis.who_pays: Large companies with over $1 billion in revenue would bear the cost of annual independent audits covering every supplier, recruiter, and raw-material source in their chains, and would risk consumer backlash when a supplier cannot be certified clean.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large companies and their supply chains

drawbacks.text: The bill sets the threshold at companies with gross annual revenues over $1 billion, so mid-size companies with the same supply-chain risks would face no audit requirement, putting them at no reputational disadvantage.

The bill requires audits, reports, and website notices but specifies no penalty for failing to conduct an audit, misreporting a result, or continuing to use suppliers found to use forced labor; it is a disclosure law without enforcement teeth.

The required notice is binary, so a company whose auditor simply cannot verify conditions deep in its chain would be forced to label its products as possibly made with child or forced labor, even absent any actual finding of abuse.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but limited: annual supply-chain audits and public homepage notices would give consumers information and pressure large brands on child and forced labor. The costs are audit and compliance expenses for very large companies. The bill's main weakness is not the burden but its design: the $1 billion threshold exempts mid-size firms, and the disclosure obligation carries no penalty for noncompliance or for ignoring what an audit finds.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to a subcommittee, and nothing further ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Juan Vargas introduced the bill on May 15, 2015, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On May 22, 2015, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade; no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded afterward.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors and no further action before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large companies with billion-dollar revenues keep operating their supply chains without an annual independent audit, a public disclosure, or the reputational risk the homepage notice would have created. Consumers and supply-chain workers gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Juan Vargas
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its sole sponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade, which held no hearing, markup, or vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no one besides the sponsor signed on, so no partisan split is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Large consumer goods, food, and retail companies with over $1 billion in revenue
industries.note: These companies would have paid for annual independent audits of their entire supply chains and faced public homepage labeling if a supplier could not be certified free of child or forced labor. A company profiting from opaque or abusive supply chains has an interest in keeping that information off its homepage.

industries.industry: Independent supply-chain audit and compliance firms
industries.note: The bill would create a recurring annual audit mandate covering every large company's supplier network, a large new market for auditors with international labor-standards experience. Their gain depends on producing honest findings for the public.

industries.industry: Agricultural producers and labor recruiters relying on child or forced labor
industries.note: Because the audit reaches labor recruiters and suppliers the company has no direct relationship with, producers using prohibited labor practices would be exposed and could lose their contracts with major brands.
